unit-alg-t2-04.title: Topic 2 · 2-4 Complex Numbers and Operations
unit-alg-t2-04.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-4: Complex Numbers and Operations

cards.def:
**The number whose square is −1: i = √−1, so i² = −1.**
• No real number squares to a negative, which is exactly why i had to be invented.
• Every square root of a negative number can be rewritten using i.
cards.hint: i exists to answer one question: what squares to a negative number?

cards.def:
**Any number of the form bi, where b is a non-zero real number.**
• Examples: 5i, −2i, 0.5i.
• An imaginary number squared always gives a negative real number.
cards.hint: An imaginary number is a real number's worth of "i" — nothing more.

cards.def:
**Any number of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers.**
• a is the real part, b is the imaginary part.
• Complex numbers include all real numbers (when b = 0) and all imaginary numbers (when a = 0) as special cases.
cards.hint: Complex numbers are the umbrella — real and imaginary numbers are both special cases of them.

cards.def:
**Combine the real parts together, and combine the imaginary parts together — same idea as combining like terms.**
• (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i.
• When subtracting, distribute the negative sign across BOTH parts of the second number first.
cards.hint: Real parts with real parts, i-parts with i-parts — never mix the two.

cards.def:
**Distribute like binomials, then replace i² with −1 wherever it appears.**
• (a + bi)(c + di) expands the same way (x + y)(z + w) would.
• The i² term is what turns into a real number and combines with the other real term.
cards.hint: FOIL it exactly like a binomial, then remember i² is secretly −1 in disguise.

cards.def:
**Two complex numbers with the same real part and opposite imaginary parts — like a + bi and a − bi.**
• Their product is always a real number: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².
• This is exactly why they're used to divide by a complex number.
cards.hint: Same real part, flipped sign on the imaginary part — that's the whole definition.

cards.def:
**Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.**
• This is the same trick as rationalizing a denominator with a square root.
• Once the denominator is real, split the result into a real part and an imaginary part.
cards.hint: You can't leave i in a denominator — the conjugate trick is how you clear it out.

cards.def:
**x² + y² factors as (x + yi)(x − yi), using complex numbers.**
• Over the real numbers, a sum of two squares can't be factored at all.
• Complex numbers make the impossible factoring possible — the same way i made the impossible square root possible.
cards.hint: A sum of squares is really a DIFFERENCE of squares in disguise — x² − (−y²) — once you allow i.

cards.def:
**When the square root in a solution method lands on a negative number, the solutions are complex, not real.**
• x² = −k (for positive k) has solutions x = ±i√k.
• A quadratic with no real solutions still ALWAYS has exactly two complex solutions.
cards.hint: A quadratic that looks unsolvable over the reals is never actually unsolvable — it just needs complex numbers.

cards.term: Example: simplifying a square root of a negative
cards.def:
**√−49 = 7i.**
• Split it: √−49 = √49 · √−1 = 7 · i.
• The real number under the root (49) becomes the coefficient; the negative sign becomes i.
cards.hint: Always pull the negative sign out FIRST, as its own separate factor of −1.

questions.q: What is the value of i²?
questions.hint: This is the defining property of i.
steps: i is defined as the square root of −1.
Squaring both sides: i² = (√−1)² = −1.
So i² = −1.

ex.main: **−1.** This one fact is what every complex-number operation eventually reduces to.

questions.q: What is √−49 written in terms of i?
questions.hint: Split the negative sign out from the number first.
steps: Rewrite √−49 as √49 · √−1.

ex.main: **7i.** The real square root (7) becomes the coefficient; the negative sign becomes i.

questions.q: Which of these is a complex number in the form a + bi?
questions.hint: It needs both a real part and an imaginary part, written with i to the first power.
steps: A complex number has the shape a + bi, with real numbers a and b.
−6 + 4i has a real part (−6) and an imaginary part (4i) — exactly that shape.
4i² actually simplifies to a real number (−4), and the other two options are missing an explicit bi term.

ex.main: **−6 + 4i.** It's written in exactly the a + bi shape, with a = −6 and b = 4.

questions.q: What is the sum of (5 − 3i) and (−2 + 8i)?
questions.hint: Add the real parts together, then add the imaginary parts together.
steps: Combine the real parts: 5 + (−2) = 3.
Combine the imaginary parts: −3i + 8i = 5i.
The sum is 3 + 5i.

questions.q: What is the difference (7 + 2i) − (4 − 6i)?
questions.hint: Distribute the negative sign across both parts of the second number before combining.
steps: Distribute the subtraction: (7 + 2i) − (4 − 6i) = 7 + 2i − 4 + 6i.
Combine the real parts: 7 − 4 = 3.
Combine the imaginary parts: 2i + 6i = 8i. The difference is 3 + 8i.

ex.main: **3 + 8i.** Forgetting to distribute the negative to BOTH terms of the second number is the most common error here.

questions.q: What is the product (3 − 4i)(2 + 5i)?
questions.hint: Distribute like two binomials, then replace i² with −1.
steps: Replace i² with −1: −20i² becomes −20(−1) = 20.

ex.main: **26 + 7i.** The i² term is what turns a leftover imaginary-looking piece into a real number — always handle it before combining.

questions.q: What is the product −3i(6 − 2i)?
questions.hint: Distribute −3i across both terms, then simplify i².
steps: Distribute: −3i(6) + (−3i)(−2i) = −18i + 6i².
Replace i² with −1: 6i² becomes 6(−1) = −6.
Combine: −6 − 18i.

questions.q: What is the complex conjugate of 4 + 9i?
questions.hint: Keep the real part the same; flip only the sign of the imaginary part.
steps: The complex conjugate keeps the real part identical.
It flips the sign of the imaginary part only.
So the conjugate of 4 + 9i is 4 − 9i.

questions.q: What is the product of the complex conjugates (4 + 9i) and (4 − 9i)?
questions.hint: The product of complex conjugates is always a real number: a² + b².
steps: The imaginary terms cancel: −36i + 36i = 0.
Replace −81i² with −81(−1) = 81. So the result is 16 + 81 = 97.

ex.main: **97.** Every pair of complex conjugates multiplies to a real number — this is exactly the property that makes them useful for dividing.

questions.q: What is the quotient 12 ⁄ (3 − i), written in the form a + bi?
questions.hint: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, 3 + i.
steps: Multiply by the conjugate over itself: 12/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i).
The denominator becomes (3 − i)(3 + i) = 9 + 1 = 10. The numerator becomes 12(3 + i) = 36 + 12i.
Divide every term by 10: 36/10 + 12i/10 = 18/5 + 6/5 i.

ex.main: **18/5 + 6/5 i.** Multiplying by the conjugate is what clears i out of the denominator — the same move as rationalizing a square root.

questions.q: How can the expression x² + 64 be factored using complex numbers?
questions.hint: Rewrite 64 as −(−64), then as (8i)².
steps: Rewrite x² + 64 as a difference of squares: x² − (−64).
Since −64 = (8i)², this is x² − (8i)².
A difference of squares factors as (x + 8i)(x − 8i).

ex.main: **(x + 8i)(x − 8i).** A sum of two squares can't be factored over the real numbers at all — this is a factorization complex numbers make possible.

questions.q: How can the expression 4x² + 9 be factored using complex numbers?
questions.hint: 4x² is (2x)², and 9 is 3² — find the complex factors from there.
steps: Rewrite as a difference of squares: 4x² − (−9) = (2x)² − (3i)², since −9 = (3i)².
A difference of squares factors as (first + second)(first − second).

ex.main: **(2x + 3i)(2x − 3i).** Check by expanding: (2x)² − (3i)² = 4x² − 9i² = 4x² + 9. ✓

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 81 = 0?
questions.hint: Isolate x², then take the square root of both sides — expect an imaginary result.
steps: Isolate x²: x² = −81.
Take the square root of both sides: x = ±√−81.
√−81 = 9i, so the solutions are x = 9i and x = −9i.

ex.main: **x = 9i and x = −9i.** A quadratic that can't be solved over the reals still has exactly two complex solutions.

questions.q: What are the solutions of 4x² + 49 = 0?
questions.hint: Isolate x² completely before taking the square root — don't forget to divide by 4.
steps: Isolate x²: 4x² = −49, so x² = −49/4.
Take the square root of both sides: x = ±√(−49/4).
√(−49/4) = (7/2)i, so the solutions are x = 7/2 i and x = −7/2 i.

ex.main: **x = ±7/2 i.** Dividing by the leading coefficient BEFORE taking the square root is the step that's easy to skip.

questions.q: How can you solve x² − 6x + 13 = 0 using factoring with complex numbers?
opts: x² − 6x + 13 factors as (x − 13)(x + 1), giving real solutions
There is no way to solve this equation
questions.hint: Try writing the left side as a perfect square plus a constant.
steps: Rewrite x² − 6x + 13 by completing the square: x² − 6x + 9 + 4 = (x − 3)² + 4.
Set this equal to 0: (x − 3)² + 4 = 0, so (x − 3)² = −4.
Take the square root of both sides: x − 3 = ±2i, so x = 3 ± 2i.

ex.main: **x = 3 ± 2i.** Rewriting as a perfect square plus a constant is exactly the completing-the-square move, and it works the same way even when the result is complex.

questions.q: Amir says the graph of y = x² + 16 has −4 as a zero. Is Amir correct?
opts: No — the equation x² + 16 = 0 has no real solutions at all
Yes, x = −4 makes the equation true
No — the only real zero is x = 4
Yes, both x = 4 and x = −4 are zeros
questions.hint: Try substituting x = −4 into x² + 16 and see what you actually get.
steps: Substitute x = −4 into x² + 16: (−4)² + 16 = 16 + 16 = 32, not 0.
In fact, x² = −16 has no real solution at all, since no real number squares to a negative.
So Amir is incorrect — this function has no REAL zeros; its zeros are the complex numbers 4i and −4i.

ex.main: **No — x² + 16 = 0 has no real solutions.** Its actual zeros, 4i and −4i, are complex, not real — the graph never touches the x-axis at all.

questions.q: What is the real part of the complex number −8 + 3i?
questions.hint: The real part is the piece without an i attached.
steps: A complex number a + bi has a real part, a, and an imaginary part, b.
In −8 + 3i, the part without i is −8.
So the real part is −8.

ex.main: **−8.** The real part never carries an i — that's what makes it real.

questions.q: What is the sum 4.5i − 4.5 + 3.5i + 2.5, written in the form a + bi?
questions.hint: Group all the real terms together, and all the i terms together, before combining.
steps: Group the real terms: −4.5 + 2.5 = −2.
Group the imaginary terms: 4.5i + 3.5i = 8i.
Combined: −2 + 8i.

ex.main: **−2 + 8i.** Even scattered out of order, real and imaginary terms still only ever combine with their own kind.

questions.q: Tamara says raising i to any integer power always results in either 1 or −1. Is Tamara correct?
opts: No — i¹ = i and i³ = −i, which are neither 1 nor −1
Yes, since i² = −1, every power of i must also be 1 or −1
Yes, because i is defined as a square root
No — every power of i is a different, unrelated number
questions.hint: Compute i¹, i², i³, and i⁴ directly and compare.
steps: i¹ = i, which is neither 1 nor −1.
i² = −1 (matches Tamara's claim), but i³ = i² · i = −1 · i = −i, which is neither 1 nor −1 either.
i⁴ = i² · i² = (−1)(−1) = 1. So the powers of i actually cycle through i, −1, −i, 1 — not just 1 and −1.

ex.main: **No.** The powers of i cycle through four values — i, −1, −i, 1 — repeating every four powers, not just two.

questions.q: Which of the following is an imaginary number?
questions.hint: An imaginary number has NO real part at all.
steps: An imaginary number has the form bi, with no separate real part — b = 0's counterpart is missing entirely, not just equal to 0 and written out.
5 + 2i has a nonzero real part (5), so it's a complex number but not a purely imaginary one.
6 and −7 are real numbers, with no i at all. Only −7i has the pure bi form of an imaginary number.

ex.main: **−7i.** It's entirely made of i, with no leftover real part — that's what makes it purely imaginary rather than just complex.
